planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all danger of frost into warm, moist (not necessarily flooded) soil; unlike paddy rices, Loto can be grown as a dryland crop with regular irrigation rather than standing water.

directions: Loto is a short-grained, awnless upland rice from the Emilia-Romagna region of northern Italy, traditionally used for risotto rather than steamed rice. It tillers freely into compact clumps on lodging-resistant stalks and, unlike most rice grown in the United States, does not need to be flooded — consistent moisture and warm soil are enough to bring it to maturity in a single temperate growing season. Home growers in cooler climates have had success direct-seeding it alongside a nurse crop of fast-germinating radish to mark the slow-emerging rice rows. Its easy-to-thresh, easy-to-hull grain makes it a practical choice for small-scale growers without dedicated rice processing equipment.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into moist, fertile soil; its extremely early maturity makes it one of the more forgiving upland rices for short-season northern gardens.

directions: Kyzyl Shala is a landrace upland rice from Uzbekistan prized for being one of the earliest-ripening rices available to home growers, often setting harvestable grain within about three months of transplanting. Its long, colorful awns are a landrace trait that helps deter birds from stripping the ripening panicles, a useful feature for gardeners without netting. Plants stay compact and stand well without lodging, and the purplish hulls with light brown bran make it easy to spot at harvest time. Because it does not require flooding, it can be grown as a dryland crop with attentive watering rather than a true paddy.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into moist, fertile soil once the weather has warmed; stake or support in exposed sites since tall stands can lodge after heavy rain.

directions: Sputnik is a modern awnless upland rice bred in Primorsky Krai in the Russian Far East, a region with a climate cool enough that it has proven workable for temperate North American gardens. It produces a short-grain brown rice and tillers vigorously, giving good yields per plant, though its taller stature makes it somewhat prone to lodging in wind and heavy rain. Start seed indoors and transplant it out once the soil has warmed, since like most upland rices it is slow to establish from seed and needs a head start against weeds. It is best suited to gardeners already growing other upland rice types who want a taller, higher-tillering variety to diversify their planting.

planting.note: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, then thin to final spacing; sorghum germinates poorly in cold soil so waiting an extra week or two past last frost pays off.

directions: Wheatland is an open-pollinated heirloom grain sorghum, sometimes marketed as milo, that produces large, well-filled heads of round, off-white seed on stalks 6 to 7 feet tall. It is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the same hot, dry conditions that stress corn, making it a reliable backup grain crop in areas prone to summer dry spells. The dried grain can be ground into a gluten-free flour or cracked for cereal, and the mature stalks and leftover heads make useful livestock and poultry feed. Harvest whole heads once the seed has hardened and the plant has begun to dry down, then thresh and winnow before storage.

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed well past last frost; Early Hegari's short season also allows a second, later planting in long-summer regions.

directions: Early Hegari is an open-pollinated grain sorghum released in 1940 and valued for combining a short growing season with a compact, broad-leafed plant only 3 to 4 feet tall, making it easy to manage in a home garden bed rather than a field. Its open heads carry white grain with a pink blush, and the plant is notably drought-tolerant and tolerant of poor soils, producing sweet, juicy stalks along the way. Because it matures faster than most grain sorghums, it is a good option for gardeners with shorter summers or those wanting to fit a grain crop into a succession planting. Harvest heads once grain has reached hard dough stage and dried down, then thresh and store the seed for flour, cereal, or poultry feed.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring while the soil is still cool, barely covering the tiny seed; Temuco tolerates light frost as a seedling but grows best where summers are mild.

directions: Temuco is a lowland coastal quinoa selected from an isolated population near Temuco in Chile's Araucania region, and it has proven to be one of the easier quinoas for cool, maritime climates because it sets seed reliably at low elevation and short day length. Its small, pale, cream-colored seed carries unusually little bitter saponin coating compared to many other quinoas, which cuts down on the rinsing needed before cooking. Grow it like other quinoas in average, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give plants room to branch, and watch for birds as the heavy seed heads ripen and dry in late summer. Cut whole panicles once the leaves have dropped and seed rubs free easily, then dry further indoors before threshing.

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early and transplant out; this millet grows fast enough to still produce a crop after a late, cool spring ruins corn.

directions: Indian Pearl Millet is a grain-type strain of pearl millet grown for its distinctive blue-grey seed rather than for forage, producing corn-like stalks topped with dense, cattail-shaped seed heads. It is markedly drought-tolerant and grows quickly enough to take advantage of short windows of good weather, often outperforming corn or wheat in a poor season. The grain is naturally gluten-free and notably high in protein, potassium, and B vitamins, and can be ground into flour, cooked whole as a porridge grain, or left for backyard poultry to forage. Cut whole seed heads once the grain has hardened and dried, then thresh by rubbing the heads between gloved hands or over a screen.
